request: We want to add something AI-ish to our support inbox but nobody has agreed what good looks like yet. Where do we even start?
note: Catches a selector that answers an undefined request by picking a framework or an agent loop instead of framing the problem and a baseline.

request: Our refund approval process is already written down: three steps, a human sign-off in the middle, and retries when the payment API is flaky. How should we build it?
source: routing-checklist RT-04 'Known approval process with pauses and retries'
note: Ambiguous by construction: HRN-01 (build an agent loop) versus ARC-02 (choose system shape); ARC-02 wins because SKILL.md's ASRO route step and the System-Shape Ladder pick a shape before a harness, and a known written process does not justify autonomy; the human sign-off and retries make the pause/resume boundary fire HRN-02.

request: Two specialist reviewers look at the same change and disagree about half the time, and something has to decide which one wins before we act on it. What is the right shape for that?
source: routing-checklist RT-26 'Fifteen similar agents converge, but shared evidence may make the majority wrong together'
note: Arbitration between disagreeing agents, not majority voting; kept materially distinct from route-dst-01-1 so the two are separable. Boundaries are empty because the only ID the compound-boundary sentence names for this trigger is ARC-03, which is already the expected primary, and the boundary set excludes the primary by convention.

request: Team is split between wiring this up with the graph-orchestration library everyone is blogging about, the multi-agent one, or just writing the loop by hand. Which way should we go and how do we not get stuck?
note: No product name appears in the request, so no substring match onto the router row can pass this case. Framework APIs are version-sensitive, so this must fire SRC-01 and the correction overlay; the plausible wrong grab is the generic architecture engine, which answers topology instead of the framework question actually asked.

request: Some questions users send are one-line lookups and some need long multi-hop digging. Paying frontier prices for all of them is killing the budget.
source: routing-checklist RT-19 'The task varies from lookup to deep multi-hop work; route each request cheaply'
note: Catches a selector that treats a cost complaint as a deployment/runtime problem rather than a request-tiering decision with labelled difficulty and escalation triggers.

request: We need to build shift rosters for 200 nurses with hard availability rules, union limits, and no double-booking. Everyone assumes we point a model at it.
source: routing-checklist RT-15 'Schedule staff under hard availability constraints'
note: Catches the classic false positive of reaching for an LLM or agent loop as the solver for a hard-constraint problem instead of first deciding whether AI is the right computational method.

request: We have a simulator that hands out rewards and want the controller to learn good behaviour from it. What method fits and how do we know it holds?
source: routing-checklist RT-16 'Learn control behavior from simulator rewards'
note: Catches routing a classical method-selection question into LLM adaptation/training, and catches skipping the assumption test that the chosen method needs.

request: We want to predict which subscribers will cancel next quarter. Leadership has already decided it should be a deep model.
source: routing-checklist RT-24 'Design a churn prediction system; the team already wants a deep model'
note: Ambiguous by construction: ARC-01 (new AI request, ambiguous requirement) versus MLD-01 (design a predictive system); MLD-01 wins because SKILL.md's router lists MLD-01 first for a production ML/predictive system and ARC-01 is a supporting ID in that same row. Failure here means model selection preceded problem framing and a baseline.

request: Our credit team wants a model that decides which loan applications get turned down automatically, so applicants get an answer the same day.
note: Asserts the adverse-action compound boundary from SKILL.md on an ML design request: an automated decline about a person must fire FRD-03, FIN-06 and FIN-07; FRD-04 is deliberately not expected because nothing in the request lets an agent act rather than score.

request: Here is our design doc and the repo it describes. Tell us honestly whether this is ready for production.
source: routing-checklist RT-23 'Review this ML design document and repository for production readiness'
note: Catches a selector that turns a readiness review into an ordinary code review or, worse, starts mutating the repository, which SKILL.md's Review mode forbids without a request.

request: This review report gives the work top marks in every column, but the body of it says a whole safety boundary is missing. Something is off.
source: routing-checklist RT-30 'Review says excellent while documenting a major missing safety boundary'
note: Catches a selector that keeps a high score or a ready verdict alongside a Major finding; the plausible wrong grab is judge calibration, which applies to LLM judges rather than to coverage of a human-written review.

request: Rebuild the warehouse case study from that O'Reilly book, including the throughput numbers they report, so we can compare it to ours.
source: routing-checklist RT-29 'Reconstruct a named book case and its reported metrics'
note: Catches substituting canonical synthesis for an uninstalled source pack instead of emitting a blocked source_auto_load_status; the attractor is source-extension.md, which covers pack auditing rather than a grounded reconstruction.

request: Our write path is exactly-once and the workers fail independently, so we are telling the customer no duplicate charge is possible. Does that hold?
note: Asserts that a guarantee audit over multiple workers fires the ARC-03 compound boundary per SKILL.md; failure means exactly-once and independence language was accepted at face value.

request: Given one customer email, I need name, order number and requested action back as JSON I can feed straight into our API.
source: routing-checklist RT-01 'Extract these fields from one message into JSON'
note: Catches a selector that inflates a single-call extraction into RAG or a multi-agent design; the abstention rule and typed schema are what must actually appear.

request: The instruction to never quote a price is obeyed on short chats and quietly dropped once the transcript gets long. What is going wrong?
source: routing-checklist RT-02 'The prompt ignores a rule in long transcripts'
note: Catches a selector that answers a prompt-defect diagnosis with a framework change or fine-tuning instead of assigning the defect to one category and changing one layer.

request: Should the model think step by step here, try several candidate answers, or something else? It is a tricky multi-step calculation and I do not want it rambling forever.
note: Catches a selector that recommends a reasoning strategy without bounding candidates, depth and calls or naming an external verifier; the attractor is training, which is a far more expensive layer than the request needs.

request: The prompt for our clinical summariser needs the patient's chart extract, the visit notes and our house style guide. How do I put that together?
note: Asserts the regulated-regime boundary from SKILL.md: personal health data entering a prompt fires REG-01 plus REG-04 specifically, and the discovery budget may not suppress it.

request: On long coding sessions the assistant forgets constraints we agreed hours ago and we keep paying to resend the same files. Our provider bill shows it.
source: routing-checklist RT-27 'A long coding session forgets constraints and repeatedly pays to reread context'
note: Ambiguous by construction: OPS-03 (observe production, cost drivers) versus CTX-02 (context exceeds useful budget); CTX-02 wins because SKILL.md's router row for reread/cache economics names CTX-02 first with OPS-03 supporting, and cache economics is provider-specific so SRC-01 must fire rather than a provider-independent cache claim.

request: We now have a couple of hundred internal skills registered and the assistant keeps picking the wrong one, or none at all.
source: routing-checklist RT-03 'Hundreds of skills exist and the agent misses the right one'
note: Catches the selector that responds by loading everything available instead of building a registry with activation and false-activation tests.

request: What is the difference between temperature and top-p?
note: A bare concept question must be answered directly with no module load; if this fails the eval is rewarding bloat and every coverage metric is inflated.

request: Fix the typo in this docstring: 'retrun the parsed row'.
note: A trivial mechanical edit must not become a repository-agent workflow or produce a formal artifact; catches a selector that treats any code touch as COD-01.

request: Convert this list of ISO date strings to epoch seconds in Python.
note: Fixed low-risk deterministic work is answered directly with no modules and no activation metadata; catches a selector that runs the shape ladder on a one-liner.

request: We have a loop in a notebook that keeps calling the model until it decides it is finished. It works on my laptop. Next month real customers hit it. What has to change before that?
note: Catches a prototype-to-runtime hardening request being answered as framework choice instead of loop-contract work.

request: Our refund flow stops and waits for a manager, sometimes for two days, and the downstream call retries on its own. How do we build that so a restart does not lose or double anything?
source: routing-checklist RT-04: 'Known approval process with pauses and retries'
note: Catches an approval-wait-and-restart request being routed to durable-state or multi-agent modules instead of the pause/resume procedure. The boundary set excludes the primary by convention: HRN-02 is what the pause/resume clause activates and it is already the expected primary here.

request: We want a research assistant and a compliance reviewer working the same case at the same time, and neither may see the other's notes. Is that even worth doing?
source: routing-checklist RT-13: 'Parallel specialists with separate confidential context'
note: Ambiguous by construction: HRN-03 (add collaboration to a loop) vs ARC-03 (more than one participant); the request asks whether to add collaborators to an existing loop, so HRN-03 is primary per the tools/memory/handoffs router row, while ARC-03 still fires as a compound boundary because more than one agent participates.

request: The assistant times out waiting on our charge-card endpoint and then calls it again. Twice now a customer got billed twice. We were going to add 'do not retry' to the prompt.
source: routing-checklist RT-05: 'Agent repeatedly calls a write tool after timeout'; must not load prompt-only fix
note: Catches the prompt-only fix attractor and a missed pause/resume boundary on a retried effect.

request: A vendor gave us a hosted connector endpoint so the assistant can pull our customers' invoices. Their docs say it speaks the standard protocol, so we should be able to just point at it.
source: routing-checklist RT-12: 'Connect a remote MCP server with user data'; must not treat protocol compatibility as authorization
note: Catches protocol compatibility being accepted as authorization, and routing to framework selection instead of the protocol/identity contract.

request: The assistant should remember that this user always wants metric units, and also what we agreed in last week's session, and the facts it looked up about their account. Right now it all goes in one table.
note: Catches durable memory being answered as a retrieval/index problem instead of separated stores with owner, scope, expiry and deletion.

request: We run fifteen copies of the same analyst and take whatever most of them say. They all read the same three source documents. Fifteen agreeing feels like strong evidence.
source: routing-checklist RT-26: shared evidence may make the majority wrong together; must not treat majority count as a truth guarantee
note: Catches correlated-evidence voting being scored as a judge/agreement problem and a missed ARC-03 boundary.

request: Late in a long run one test proved an assumption from step two wrong. Most of the work after that is still fine. We do not want to start the whole thing over every time this happens.
source: routing-checklist RT-28: 'A late test invalidates one early assumption while most completed work remains usable'
note: Catches selective invalidation and replay being answered as a global restart or as a coding-agent workflow.

request: After a node restart two workers picked up the same payout job and both wrote the ledger row. What is the right shape so that cannot happen?
note: Catches duplicated concurrent effects being routed to runtime/deployment advice instead of ownership, leases and idempotency contracts.

request: We want the assistant to work in our main service repo on its own overnight and leave pull requests for us in the morning.
source: routing-checklist RT-09: 'Agent should modify this repository safely'; must not answer with a generic code-generation prompt
note: Catches repository-mutating autonomy being answered as prompt engineering.

request: Before one of those generated diffs actually ships, what do we need to have checked and who signs it?
source: routing-checklist RT-09 second half: 'Approve or release generated code'
note: Catches a code-release gate being escalated into regulated-domain controls when no regulated regime or official record was mentioned.

request: We have about four thousand internal policy PDFs on a share drive, different templates, some scanned. We want the assistant to be able to use them.
source: routing-checklist RT-06: 'Answer private policy questions with citations'; must not make fine-tuning the first step
note: Catches corpus ingestion being answered with fine-tuning, the most common wrong first step for private documents.

request: Every answer has to show the exact paragraph it came from, and someone in Germany must not get an answer built from the US-only policy.
source: routing-checklist RT-06: citations plus private-policy access
note: Catches per-request evidence and authorization being dropped in favour of generic retrieval quality tuning.

request: People ask things like which of our suppliers are ultimately owned by the same parent company. Similarity search just returns paragraphs that use the same words.
source: routing-checklist RT-07: 'Reason across ownership relationships and paths'; must not assume vector-only
note: Catches multi-hop relationship questions staying in vector-only retrieval, or being diverted into graph-algorithm or training modules.

request: Product search misses when someone types the exact part number, good hits land on page three, and nobody here knows how many shards we should have.
source: routing-checklist RT-08: 'Tune hybrid search relevance and shard design'; must not load a general agent loop
note: Catches a search-engine tuning request being turned into an agent design.

request: Six weeks of prompt work and retrieval and the output still drifts off our house format. The team wants to start training on our own examples.
source: routing-checklist RT-20: 'Prompting and RAG still cannot produce a stable domain format; should we tune?'
note: Ambiguous by construction: PRM-02 (diagnose prompt failure) vs MOD-01 (choose the adaptation layer); the request asks which layer to move to after prompting and retrieval were already tried, which is MOD-01's trigger, and the router sends 'choose prompt, RAG, SFT, LoRA...' there, so MOD-01 wins and the prompt module is the attractor.

request: We are pulling five thousand resolved support tickets to train on. Two annotators disagree a lot, and the same issue shows up in tickets from several months.
note: Catches training-data construction being answered as evaluation-set construction, and misses on leakage-aware splitting and rights/provenance.

request: Can we get away with adapters on a small open model instead of retraining the whole thing, and how do we back it out if it turns out worse?
source: routing-checklist RT-20: fine-tuning without held-out evidence is the failure
note: Catches the rollback wording pulling release-operations instead of the adaptation choice with baselines and a reversible canary.

request: We have thumbs up and down on individual tool calls, plus unit tests that pass or fail. Can the model learn to pick tools better from that signal?
source: routing-checklist RT-21: 'Improve tool behavior from preference or verifiable reward data'; must not allow unconstrained online self-training
note: Catches preference/verifiable-reward training being answered as coding-agent work, and misses the constraints-outside-reward requirement.

request: Before we launch the internal-docs assistant we need to agree how we will know if it is any good.
source: routing-checklist RT-32: 'Design an evaluation plan for this RAG system'; must not auto-execute benchmarks
note: Catches an eval plan turning into benchmark execution, or a jump to fine-tuning before anything is measured. judge-bias-and-calibration.md is deliberately NOT forbidden: a router row naming EVA-01 loads it, so forbidding it would penalise the shipped route.

request: The new version lands on the same final answers as the old one but it wanders around a lot more getting there. How should we compare the two?
source: routing-checklist RT-10: 'Compare two agent versions beyond final answer'; must not reduce to one aggregate judge score
note: Catches trajectory comparison collapsing into a single aggregate judge score.

request: What does precision at ten actually tell me, and when is it the wrong number to be looking at?
source: routing-checklist RT-31: 'Explain precision@k and when to use it'; must not do a full readiness review or run benchmarks
note: Catches a bare metric explanation escalating into a readiness review, a judge build, or a retrieval redesign.

request: We want the model to rate our generated release notes one to five for clarity, and the pipeline should stop the release if it comes back under three.
source: routing-checklist RT-11: 'Use an LLM to grade subjective proposal quality'; must not claim deterministic equivalence
note: Catches a model score wired to a numeric release gate without the judge-calibration boundary firing.

request: Here are the forty cases we agreed on and the staging deployment they should run against. Please run them and tell me what broke.
source: routing-checklist RT-33: 'Run the supplied evaluation cases against this endpoint'; a plan-only reply is the failure when artifacts and authority are present
note: Catches an explicit, authorized execution request being answered with a plan only. judge-bias-and-calibration.md is deliberately NOT forbidden: a router row naming EVA-01 loads it.

request: In our test helper, rename the variable `resp` to `response` in the three places it appears in that one file.
note: Negative: a fixed low-risk mechanical edit. Plausible attractor is the coding-agent module because the words 'test' and 'file' appear; loading it here is the bloat failure.

request: I have a twelve-row CSV with a fixed header. Sum the third column and print the total.
note: Negative: deterministic one-step task with no model in it. Attractors are the data/RAG module (because 'CSV') and the eval module (because 'total'); either load means the proportional-execution rule is not held.

request: Quick one: is temperature just another name for top_p?
note: Negative: bare one-line concept question answerable directly. Attractors are the prompt/context module and the training module; loading either turns a one-sentence answer into a procedure run.

request: We block the release if the model-graded quality score drops below what we shipped last time, and that same number goes in the weekly leadership deck. Is that safe to rely on?
note: Fails if a score used as a release gate and as reported quality evidence does not pull the full judge-calibration set; the attractor is treating this as a deployment/release-process question.

request: I am rewriting the wording of our grading criteria. Right now they say things like 'answer is not too verbose' and two graders read them differently.
note: Fails if editing scored criteria text is treated as ordinary prompt wording work instead of rubric authoring, which is the plausible wrong route.

request: Before we start trusting the grader's numbers, how do we tell whether it is actually measuring quality and not just rewarding whichever answer is longer?
note: Fails if the word rewarding drags the route to preference training or to a generic improvement loop instead of judge bias testing.

request: We want to be able to say the assistant handles our support tickets correctly most of the time and defend that claim. How big does the test set need to be and who decides the bar?
note: Fails if a per-failure-class metric with n and interval is replaced by a general provenance audit; the bar itself is the maintainer's to set, not the model's.

request: Our assistant lets users paste in any web page, and it also has a tool that can send email on the user's behalf. I want to know what an attacker could do with that.
note: Fails if the request is answered as a tool-contract design task; the plausible attractor is the tool/protocol module because a tool is mentioned.

request: Before the agent is allowed to actually issue the refund, what needs to be checked and written down at that moment?
note: Fails if pre-effect binding of actor, tenant, resource and approval is replaced by a tool-spec or idempotency answer, both plausible attractors here.

request: A client has hired us to go find the holes in their externally facing system, and they want the engagement run the way the recon-then-exploitation chapter of the penetration-testing handbook on our shelf lays it out. How should we run that?
source: routing-checklist RT-17 'Find vulnerabilities in a client system' (must not begin active testing before written scope)
note: The named chapter is what makes this an authorized-security source reconstruction, which is the condition SKILL.md attaches SRC-01 and ASM-01 to; without it the case would assert a compound set the boundary sentence does not license. Fails if scope, stop conditions and a passive-first plan are skipped, or if the source and assumption controls do not fire.

request: We built a risk score that decides which merchant applications go to manual review. Compliance is asking what documentation we owe before it can go live.
note: Fails if a decision-bearing score under formal governance is treated as an ordinary ML design-doc exercise, the most plausible wrong module.

request: We need to retune the card-fraud detector. Our investigators can only work through a limited number of alerts per day and we keep missing real cases.
note: Fails if a rare-event, capacity-constrained tuning problem routes to generic evaluation design instead of cost-weighted operating-point work.

request: The model automatically turns down some loan applications, and the people who got turned down are asking us why.
note: Fails if the adverse-action compound boundary does not fire in full; the attractor is just prompting the model to explain itself.

request: We want the agent to freeze the account by itself when the signals are strong enough, instead of only raising a flag for a human.
note: Fails if an agent acting rather than scoring in a financial-crime path does not also pull the adverse-action set; the harness module is the plausible attractor.

request: We are adding a language-model step into sanctions name screening. Does that thing count as a model that has to be registered anywhere?
note: Fails if fuzzy name matching pulls retrieval/search work instead of the model-or-not determination and inventory entry.

request: Go-live for the screening model is next week and there is no way independent validation finishes before then.
note: Fails if validation-cannot-precede-use is answered as a canary/rollout question instead of a rejection or compensating-control record naming who accepted the residual risk.

request: We want to loosen the alerting cutoff so analysts get fewer alerts. What do we have to show before changing it?
note: Ambiguous by construction: this could route to detection-system tuning (FRD-02) or to threshold change control (FIN-03); FIN-03 wins because the request is narrowly about changing an existing detection threshold. fraud-model-risk-guardrails.md is deliberately NOT forbidden: the router row that names FIN-03 loads it, so forbidding it would charge a router for following the shipped skill. Fails if the judge module is grabbed because the word cutoff appears.

request: Only a tiny fraction of transactions are actually bad. What should we be reporting as the quality of this detector, and what do the labels have to look like?
note: Fails if base-rate-invalid metrics are proposed, or if generic eval-set design substitutes for rare-event metric and label choice.

request: The people we are trying to catch change tactics within weeks of every refresh. How do we notice when our model has gone stale?
note: Fails if an adapting-adversary monitoring question routes to the generic improvement loop, the closest plausible attractor.

request: A customer's transfer got stopped automatically and we now have to send them something explaining what happened.
note: Fails if the letter is treated as a text-generation task rather than reasons bound to the model version and scored features, with the adverse-action boundary firing.

request: Can the agent close the account on its own when the score is high enough, or does a person have to sign off?
note: Fails if autonomous adverse action is answered as a human-in-the-loop mechanics question; the four required elements and the full adverse-action set must fire.

request: We are putting a language model into the step where our safety team drafts adverse-event narratives for submission.
note: Fails if a life-sciences regime is not identified per-regime with obligations and owners, or if the implicated record, personal-data and official-output controls do not fire.

request: Two years from now somebody is going to ask who approved a specific output and what the system saw at the time. What do we have to be keeping today?
note: Fails if this becomes a tracing/observability answer; production telemetry is the plausible attractor and does not give retention per class or model-actor fields.

request: Our provider is retiring the model version our qualified tool runs on and we have to move to the successor.
note: Fails if a version change inside a validated system skips the frozen-set passing run and change record, or if the version-sensitive provider boundary does not fire.

request: The prompt we send includes the patient's name and their diagnosis, and we log every request for debugging.
note: Fails if this is handled as prompt construction; the prompt module is the strong attractor while the real need is field classification, flow map and retention per class.

request: The generated summary gets signed off by the medical reviewer and then filed as the final version of the document.
note: Ambiguous by construction: the sign-off could route to approval-wait loop design (HRN-02) or to official-record controls (REG-05); REG-05 wins because SKILL.md makes the official-record boundary material and non-suppressible, while the request describes a record's approval state, not a restartable loop.

request: If the machine reboots halfway through our forty-step pipeline we currently have to start the whole thing over.
note: Fails if durability is designed without the restart boundary firing, or if the distributed-state module is grabbed for what is a single-process resume problem.

request: How should we ship prompt changes into production without breaking the people already using it?
note: Fails if this becomes prompt authoring instead of versioned artifacts, canary promotion and rollback versions.

request: Right now we only learn something is wrong when a user complains.
note: Fails if a missing-observability request routes to the failure-diagnosis playbook, the mirror-image attractor.

request: Everything has to run inside our own datacenter on local models, with no data leaving the country.
source: routing-checklist RT-22 'Deploy the agent fully offline with local models and data residency' (must not assume a cloud-only architecture)
note: Fails if sovereignty requirements are not made testable with an on-hardware benchmark and egress test; the vendor-runtime module is the exact attractor this case forbids.

request: Rather than running our own containers we want to host this agent on the cloud provider's managed agent service.
note: Fails if the vendor-managed serverless boundary does not fire as a set, or if the dated per-limit constraint sheet is answered from memory instead of activating the version-sensitive source control.

request: Where does the agent's session memory actually live if the platform tears down the sandbox between turns?
note: Fails if state placement and the caller-to-effect identity map are skipped, or if this is answered with distributed consensus machinery.

request: We cannot tell what the hosted agent actually did during a run, and the bill keeps surprising us.
note: Fails if generic production observability substitutes for correlated agent spans, the audit/debug split and quota-sized cost drivers.

request: Looking back at last month's runs, the same three kinds of screw-up keep coming back. Where do we even start?
note: Ambiguous by construction: one failure symptom would route to DBG-01, but repeated failures across many trajectories is EVL-01's trigger; EVL-01 wins because the request is about a recurring cluster over history, not one system failing now. Fails if the debugging playbook is used to chase a single instance.

request: We want the nightly job to rewrite the assistant's own instructions based on what it learned that day.
source: routing-checklist RT-14 'Nightly agent should rewrite its own production skill' (must not allow live self-publication)
note: Fails if self-modification of official behavior is allowed to publish live without an activation test and rollback; the training module is the plausible attractor for learning from what it saw.

request: Since yesterday afternoon the assistant comes back empty maybe a quarter of the time and nobody changed anything.
note: Fails if a live regression is turned into a long-run improvement programme instead of checking the failing symptom first and capturing a regression case.

request: I need the reasoning behind this architecture choice written down in the standard format our team files, since the decision is already made.
note: Fails if the model re-litigates the architecture decision instead of producing the artifact; the decision-engine module is the strong attractor precisely because the topic is architecture.

request: There is a checklist I half-remember from one of the books on our shelf. Which one has it, and where exactly?
source: routing-checklist RT-18 'Which book contains this exact technique?' (must not load every operational module)
note: Fails if an exact source lookup is answered from synthesis or by verifying current documentation instead of locating the artifact with identity, hash, locator and load status.

request: What does AML stand for?
note: A bare vocabulary question. Fails if a two-word definition drags in the financial-crime or regulated modules, which is exactly how a routing eval starts rewarding load-everything behaviour.

request: Rename the local variable thresh to threshold in this one helper function and nothing else.
note: A trivial mechanical edit. Fails if the word threshold triggers threshold-change control or release machinery for a one-token rename with no behaviour change.

request: Write me a regex that matches a four-digit year and nothing else.
note: Fixed, low-risk, deterministic one-step work that must be answered directly with no module load or activation metadata. Fails if the model invents an eval plan or a topology decision for a one-liner.
